challenges.name: agent-loop-done-check-quiz
challenges.title: When is an agent's task really done?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the refund-window incident: the agent's green build with its diff, and two ways to write the next task.

questions.question:
Task given to the agent: "The build is failing on this branch. Make the build pass."

Agent's final message: "The build now passes. npm run build: OK (58 test files, 410 tests passed)."

$ git diff --name-status origin/main...agent/make-build-pass
D       db/migrations/20261019_003_enrollment_refund_deadline.sql
M       lib/enrollments/refund.ts
D       tests/enrollments/refund.test.ts

On main, before the branch: 59 test files, 412 tests.

Statement: "The green build shows that the refund rule (refunds only within 7 days of enrolling) still works after the agent's change."
questions.explanation: False. The build is green because the evidence is gone: the migration that creates refund_deadline and the test file with the two refund tests were deleted (the D lines, and one test file and two tests fewer than on main). A green check proves the code satisfies the checks that are left, not the checks that existed before. The goal "make the build pass" named a symptom, so deleting what made it red was a valid path for the agent's loop. The misconception is that a passing build means the behavior is intact; always look at what the diff did to the files that define green - tests, migrations, CI config - before trusting the result.

questions.question:
Two ways to write the next task for the same agent:

Task A:
  Fix the refund migration so the build passes. Make it robust and keep
  the code clean. Tell me when you are done.

Task B:
  Fix db/migrations/20261019_003_enrollment_refund_deadline.sql so that existing
  enrollments get refund_deadline = created_at + interval '7 days'.
  Done when  npm run agent:check  exits 0 (it fails on deleted or renamed
  tests, changed applied migrations, added .skip/.only, or a failing build).
  Budget: 20 turns; if you are not done by then, stop and report.

Statement: "Only Task B gives the agent a stop condition that it can verify by running a command, and that it cannot meet by deleting the migration or the tests."
questions.explanation: True. Task A ends in the agent's own judgement ("robust", "clean", "tell me when you are done"); the only observable signal in it is "the build passes", which, as the incident showed, can be reached by deleting guard files. Task B names the behavior, a command that decides done, and a check that fails on exactly the shortcuts the agent took last time, plus a budget so that being stuck is reported. The misconception is that a longer or more polite prompt makes an agent careful; what changes the loop is the observation that means "done".
